Reporting network regression results

Source: R/report_models.R
netreg_results.Rd

These methods report a netreg, the result of estimate_mrqap(), whether its class is netreg_lm, netreg_glm, or netreg_css.

  • print() shows the result in three parts: a title that says what was fitted, tidy() of the estimates with significance marks, and a footer that says how the null distribution was made and the controls that differ from the default. At options(snet_verbosity = "debug"), the footer also names the methods that give more.

  • summary() gives the full table of the coefficients: the columns of tidy(), the lower and upper permutation p-values, a plain title of each effect, and the parts of each term. Its print leaves out title and the parts, which are too wide to read there, and adds the random intercepts of a mixed model, glance(), the unobserved dyads of each variable, and the terms that the formula dropped or changed, each after a blank line. glance() gives the permutations and the number of dyads, so the footer does not say them again.

  • tidy() and glance() give the results as a tibble, after {broom}: one row for each coefficient, and one row for the whole model. So an MRQAP result can sit in one table beside an ERGM or a SIENA one (see other_results).

  • nobs() gives the number of dyads that the model used: unobserved dyads, fixed ties, and the loops that the model leaves out are not counted.

  • logLik() and deviance() give the log-likelihood and the deviance of the observed model, so AIC() and BIC() work too.

  • fitted() and residuals() give one value for each dyad that the model used, in the rows of the dyad-level data.

  • formula() gives the formula that was fitted, after specify_mrqap() read it, and terms() gives the terms of the columns that were fitted, as the coefficients name them. For the formula of chosen rows of a table of terms, see specify_terms.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'netreg_lm'
print(x, ..., print_b = FALSE, print_random = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'netreg_glm'
print(x, ..., print_b = FALSE, print_random = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'netreg_css'
print(x, ..., print_b = FALSE, print_random = FALSE)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
tidy(
  x,
  exponentiate = FALSE,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'summary_netreg'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
glance(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg_lm'
glance(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg_glm'
glance(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg_css'
glance(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
nobs(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
logLik(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
deviance(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
fitted(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
residuals(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
formula(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'netreg'
terms(x, ...)

Arguments

x, object

A netreg, from estimate_mrqap().

...

For residuals(), passed to the residuals() method of the observed model, such as type = "pearson" for a glm. For summary(), passed to tidy(), such as alternative = "greater". Otherwise not used.

print_b, print_random

Deprecated. print_b = TRUE also prints the p-values of the coefficients, rather than of their test statistics, and print_random = TRUE the random intercepts. Use summary(), which gives both.

exponentiate

Logical, whether to exponentiate the estimates, e.g. to give odds ratios for a logistic model.

alternative

Which permutation p-value to report: "two.sided" (the default) for Pr(>=|t|), "less" for Pr(<=t), or "greater" for Pr(>=t).

Value

print() returns x, invisibly. tidy(), summary(), and glance() return a tibble; the tibble of summary() has the class summary_netreg too, for its print. tidy() gives the columns term, estimate, statistic, and p.value. summary() gives these columns, p.lower and p.upper, a title that defines each effect, and the columns of the fit's term table, fit$terms: the effect (the formula term) each coefficient comes from, its layer, attribute, category, and reference category, and for an interaction its operands. These group the coefficients without parsing their names. glance() gives the fit statistics that the model keeps. nobs() gives an integer, logLik() a logLik object, deviance() a number, fitted() and residuals() a numeric vector, formula() a formula, and terms() a terms object.

Details

The p-values come from the permutations. Every other method reads the observed model, which the permutations do not change. A permutation test gives a p-value but no standard error, so tidy() and summary() have no std.error column. p.value is read from the permutations of the test statistic, as print() shows it. Where no permutation reached the observed statistic, print() shows the p-value as below 1/times, the smallest that the permutations can give, and marks it as that bound. For the confusion matrix of a binary outcome, see diagnose_confusion(). When the predictors are permuted, the intercept has no test, and its p.value is NA.

Two methods of {stats} work without a method here: coef() gives the estimates, and update() fits the model again, with a changed formula, times, or control, from the call that the result keeps.

Methods left out

  • vcov() and confint(): a covariance or an interval from the observed model would not come from the permutations, and could be read as the basis of the permutation p-values.

  • weights(): a network regression uses no weights.

  • [: a result has no rows to select. Use $ or [[ for an element.

  • profile(): a permutation fit has no likelihood to profile.

Fixed effects

A gaussian model absorbs its fixed effects by demeaning. Its log-likelihood and deviance are those of the model with a dummy for each group, and logLik() counts the absorbed parameters in its df, so that AIC(), BIC(), and glance() are those of that model too. fitted() gives the observed values less the residuals, not the demeaned fitted values.

See also

Other models: control_mrqap(), diagnose_confusion(), other_results, play_diffusions(), regression, specify, specify_terms, terms_mrqap, test_fit, test_measures, test_parameter()

Examples

css_model <- estimate_mrqap(advice ~ same(dept) + reports,
                            manynet::ison_hightech, times = 5)
css_model
#> # Logistic MRQAP of advice
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   term        estimate statistic p.value signif   
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>   <noquote>
#> 1 (Intercept)   -1.07     -38.5  NA               
#> 2 same_dept      0.552      9.53 < 0.2            
#> 3 reports        3.82      15.3  < 0.2            
#> 
#> # Null: 5 permutations of each predictor, by double semi-partialling.
#> # Permutations relabel senders, receivers, and reporters alike.
summary(css_model)
#> # Logistic MRQAP of advice
#> 
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>   term        estimate statistic p.lower p.upper p.value signif   
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl> <chr>   <chr>   <chr>   <noquote>
#> 1 (Intercept)   -1.07     -38.5  NA      NA      NA               
#> 2 same_dept      0.552      9.53 1       < 0.2   < 0.2            
#> 3 reports        3.82      15.3  1       < 0.2   < 0.2            
#> 
#> # Fit of the observed model
#>    family logLik  AIC   BIC deviance null.deviance df.residual nobs   permute
#>  binomial  -4989 9984 10005     9978         10922        8817 8820 predictor
#>  times reporters
#>      5        21
#> 
#> # Permutations relabel senders, receivers, and reporters alike.
tidy(css_model)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   term        estimate statistic p.value
#>   <chr>          <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 (Intercept)   -1.07     -38.5       NA
#> 2 same_dept      0.552      9.53       0
#> 3 reports        3.82      15.3        0
glance(css_model)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 11
#>   family   logLik   AIC    BIC deviance null.deviance df.residual  nobs permute 
#>   <chr>     <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>         <dbl>       <dbl> <int> <chr>   
#> 1 binomial -4989. 9984. 10005.    9978.        10922.        8817  8820 predict…
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: times <dbl>, reporters <int>
nobs(css_model)
#> [1] 8820
AIC(css_model)
#> [1] 9983.796
formula(css_model)
#> advice ~ same(dept) + reports
#> <environment: 0xbb3c4ee08>
head(fitted(css_model))
#> [1] 0.3723726 0.2546663 0.3723726 0.2546663 0.2546663 0.2546663
